# The Lugar Tribute  
Guangzhou, China, Qing dynasty (1644- 1911), 1910 Silk scroll with a red sandalwood casket and silver mounts, scroll: 347 x 116.5 cm, casket: height 84 cm On permanent loan from Major Richard Pinker HKU.W.2001.1393  
Embroidered against a pale- yellow background, this silk satin scroll was a gift presented to Sir Frederick Lugar (1858- 1945), the fourteenth British Governor of Hong Kong (1907- 12), by eighty- four local Chinese dandags (prominent "gentry merchants" who exchanged wealth for social status or official titles, and who were often actively involved in charitable affairs) in 1910. It was presented to Lugar in recognition of his contributions to Hong Kong, which included founding the University of Hong Kong and prohibiting the practice of abandoning corpses on the streets, which remained widespread in the nineteenth century.  
Stored in an ornately carved red sandalwood casket adorned with bat- shaped silver brackets, the scroll is delicately embroidered with auspicious motifs, such as mandarin ducks and butterflies symbolizing harmonious relationships and joyfulness. A striking pair of peacocks on the scroll, emblematic of culture and virtue according to the "Cheng Khoof of Changyi, likely echoes an inscription days zingjiang ("virtue shelters Hong Kong") on the lid of the casket, which glorifies the success and prosperity of Hong Kong during Lugar's tenure.
